explanation: Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and interpret escape sequences, while single-quoted strings do neither.
The ?? operator checks isset() semantics, so undefined variables or indexes return the right-hand value without emitting notices or warnings.
The echo construct accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and outputs them concatenated without any separator.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always returns 1, so it can be used within an expression such as $x = print "hello";
The elvis operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when the left is falsy.
In PHP, the concatenation operator (.) has lower precedence than arithmetic operators like + and -, meaning it is evaluated after them.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
`.` and `+` have the same precedence and are left-associative, so it evaluates as ('sum: ' . 2) + 3 = 'sum: 2' + 3 = 0 + 3 = 3.
The === operator requires arrays to have the same key/value pairs in the same order with identical types.
`0 == false` is a loose (non-strict) comparison that evaluates to true; only `0 === false` would be strict and return false.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number converts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 becomes "abc" == "0" which is false (this was true in PHP 7).
With loose comparison, null == 0, null == "", and null == false all evaluate to true.
PHP parses the leading numeric portion of the string before the first non-numeric character, so (int)'42abc' becomes 42.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer for the addition, resulting in 10.
In PHP, casting false to an empty string gives an empty string "" (while true becomes "1").
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, which is not identical to 0.3.
strrev() reverses bytes rather than characters, so multibyte UTF-8 sequences get corrupted.
str_contains() checks whether the second string is found within the first, and 'world' is indeed contained in 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right, left, or both sides using the STR_PAD_LEFT and STR_PAD_BOTH constants.
By default trim() strips spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs (" \t\n\r\0\x0B").
strlen counts bytes, and é is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so h(1)+é(2)+l(1)+l(1)+o(1)=6.
substr with a negative start returns the last 3 characters of the string.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character converted to uppercase, and it cannot modify the original string since PHP strings are immutable.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) interpolates variables like a double-quoted string, while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') does not.
sort() reindexes numeric keys, so use asort() to preserve key-to-value associations.
PHP casts string keys that represent integers to integer keys automatically.
in_array() performs loose (==) comparison by default; strict comparison is only used when the third parameter $strict is set to true.
Without a callback, array_filter() removes elements that evaluate to false, such as empty strings, 0, null, and false.
By default array_slice() reindexes numeric keys, so original numeric keys are not preserved unless preserve_keys is set to true.
array_slice takes 2 elements starting from index 1, giving [20, 30].
The + array union keeps keys from the left array first, so 'a' => 1 wins and 'b' is added, giving 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator, merging them like array_merge does for string keys.
In PHP 8, named arguments cannot be combined with argument unpacking (...$args) in the same function call.
In PHP, an anonymous function creates its own scope, so outer variables must be imported with the `use` keyword (only arrow functions `fn` capture automatically).
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments passed to the function, which is 3.
PHP arrow functions (fn) must have a single expression as their body and cannot use curly braces for a statement block.

PHP arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value (bound when the closure is created), not by reference at use time; capturing by reference requires a regular closure with `use (&$var)`.
A static closure has no $this context, so it cannot access or capture $this (attempting to bind it causes a fatal error).
The closure captures $x by value at creation time, so changing $x to 7 afterwards doesn't affect it.
Without strict_types, PHP coerces numeric strings like "5" to int automatically.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers in constructor parameters to declare and assign properties automatically.
The final keyword, when applied to a method, prevents it from being overridden in subclasses.
The final modifier prevents child classes from overriding the method.
Private properties are not visible to subclasses; only public and protected members are accessible.
PHP builds anonymous class names as the literal prefix "class@anonymous" followed by a NUL byte and then the file/line info, so the part before the NUL byte is "class@anonymous".
Private parent methods are excluded from inheritance, so a child can redeclare the same name with any visibility without conflict.
__get() is invoked for both non-existent properties and inaccessible (e.g. private/protected) ones, not just non-existent ones.
Modifying a readonly property after initialization raises a PHP Error ('Cannot modify readonly property'), not an Exception.
PHP interfaces can define constants (e.g., `interface A { const X = 1; }`), though they cannot have properties or method implementations.
The instanceof operator returns true if an object is an instance of a class or implements an interface.
Since PHP 8.0, interfaces may declare public static methods that implementing classes must provide.
instanceof checks whether an object is an instance of a class, a class that implements an interface, or the interface itself.
PHP interfaces may only declare method signatures (plus constants); methods with bodies are not allowed, unlike traits which provide concrete implementations.
Abstract methods may be declared public or protected (and private as of PHP 7.1), so protected visibility is perfectly valid.
The cases() method returns an array containing all defined cases of the enum, which are A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare class constants.
Since PHP 7, the Throwable interface is implemented by both Exception and Error, making them siblings under Throwable.
TypeError inherits from Error, not Exception, so it is not caught by catch (Exception $e).
The @ operator only suppresses error diagnostics (warnings/notices), not exceptions explicitly thrown with throw.
intdiv() with a zero divisor throws a DivisionByZeroError since PHP 7.
The finally block runs regardless of whether an exception is caught, and even if no exception occurs at all.
An exception thrown in a finally block replaces any return value or exception from the try block.
An object cast to bool is always true, so (bool) new Exception('x') evaluates to true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() execute when the script ends, including when exit/die is called.
The `use` statement only creates an alias and does not load the class file; the class is autoloaded when first referenced.
PHP requires the `function` keyword after `use` when importing a namespaced function, e.g. `use function Foo\bar;`.
PSR-4 strips the App\ prefix and maps the remaining sub-namespace and class name under src/ with a .php extension.
Composer's generated autoloader file calls spl_autoload_register() to register the autoloading functions for PSR-4, PSR-0, classmap, and files autoloaders.
__NAMESPACE__ is the magic constant that returns the name of the current namespace, or an empty string if in the global namespace.
An unqualified class name is resolved relative to the current namespace, not the global root; only a leading backslash forces global resolution.
PSR-4 strips the prefix App\, so Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.

Imports via `use` must appear at the outermost scope of a file (or inside a namespace block) and are resolved at compile time for the whole file; placing an import `use` inside a function is a parse error, and only closure/trait `use` is allowed in inner scopes.
In PHP, arrays are value types, so assigning one array to another variable creates a copy of the array rather than a reference to it.
PHP arrays are assigned by value (copy-on-write), so appending to $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
In PHP, variables defined in the global scope are not automatically available inside functions; you must use the global keyword, the $GLOBALS array, or pass them as parameters to access them.
$GLOBALS['x'] refers to the actual global variable itself, so unsetting it removes it globally, not just within the function.
inc() takes $x by reference and increments it, so $n becomes 6.
A by-value foreach iterates over a copy (copy-on-write) of the array, so changes made inside the loop are not reflected in the current pass — you need foreach ($arr as &$v) for live updates.
A static property belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances, so changes are visible across all objects.
PHP converts boolean array keys to integers (true becomes 1, false becomes 0), so they are never stored as bool.
Since PHP 7.0, a value can be returned from a generator and retrieved with $gen->getReturn() once the generator has completed.
Once a generator has been fully run to completion, calling rewind() throws a LogicException because it cannot be advanced again.
The yield from expression passes control to a sub-generator or iterable, delegating iteration to it until it is exhausted.
A function containing yield returns a Generator object, whose class name is Generator.
The generator yields three values (1, 2, 3), so iterator_to_array produces an array with 3 elements.
SplStack is a LIFO stack; SplQueue implements a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is an SPL class that wraps an array and implements the Iterator interface (along with ArrayAccess, Countable, and SeekableIterator) for traversal.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a cryptographically random salt, and passing a separate salt is deprecated and unnecessary.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT uses bcrypt, not md5, which is handled by the separate PASSWORD_MD5 constant.
password_verify checks the plain password against the generated hash, and since they match, it returns true.
strip_tags() only removes HTML tags and does nothing to neutralize SQL syntax; prepared statements/parameterized queries are required to prevent SQL injection.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID, which is the recommended defense against session fixation when privilege changes, such as on login.
php_sapi_name() returns the name of the Server Application Programming Interface (SAPI) currently in use, such as 'cli'.

session_destroy() only removes the session data stored on the server; the session cookie itself must be deleted separately (e.g., with setcookie() or session_unset + cookie expiration) since it is stored client-side in the browser.
session_start() must be called first to initialize the session and populate $_SESSION.
The array_find() function, along with array_find_key(), array_any(), and array_all(), was introduced in PHP 8.4.
Property hooks (the get and set syntax inside property declarations) were introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing different read/write visibilities such as public private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which warns when a function's return value is ignored, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The |> pipe operator was accepted as an RFC feature for PHP 8.5, where it first became available.
The clone-with syntax clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) for cloning with property overrides was introduced in PHP 8.5.
array_first() and array_last() are not built-in PHP functions in any version; equivalent behavior is achieved with reset()/end() or collections.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was accepted for inclusion in PHP 8.6.
The clamp_v2 RFC, which adds the clamp() function, was merged into the PHP 8.6 release cycle (per its status as of 2026-11-07).
The Context Managers RFC has not been accepted/implemented in PHP as of that date, so the claim that it is adopted is false.
The Bound-Erased Generic Types RFC was put to a vote and did not reach the required support, so it was declined.
No accepted RFC exists making Zend Thread Safety (ZTS) the default in PHP as of that date.
PHP still lacks native generic/parameterized type support even in version 8.5; generics only exist as informal annotations like PHPDoc types.
PHP 8.5 was released in November 2025 and remains the latest stable version on 2026-11-07, with PHP 8.6 scheduled for GA on 2026-11-19.
Development of PHP 6 was abandoned due to Unicode/encoding issues, so PHP 5.6 was followed directly by PHP 7.0 in December 2015.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute was accepted and introduced in PHP 8.4 to deprecate functions, methods, and class constants in a structured way.
Both architectures require that inner layers (domain/core) never reference outer layers, so all dependencies point inward toward the center.
Domain entities should remain framework-agnostic, depending only on the language itself and possibly the standard library, to keep the domain layer pure and testable.
Controllers belong to the delivery/presentation layer and Twig templates to the view layer; business logic lives in the domain/use-case layer.
In onion architecture the innermost layer is the domain model/entities, which contains the core business rules and has no dependencies on outer layers.
Tools like deptrac statically analyze layer dependencies and fail builds when forbidden cross-layer calls are detected.
Clean architecture requires use cases to depend only on abstract ports/DTOs, not on framework details like HTTP requests or an EntityManager.
A repository exposes collections of aggregates/entities behind an interface, hiding the persistence mechanism.

Clean architecture isolates database specifics behind repository interfaces in the outer layer, so replacing PostgreSQL only requires changing the infrastructure implementation while domain and use case code remain untouched.
An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a consistency boundary, not a database table.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Value Object has no identity, is immutable, and equality is determined by comparing its attribute values.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the single entry point through which all external access and modifications of the aggregate's objects must be made.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories manage whole aggregates via their root, ensuring consistency boundaries.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is a common language shared by developers and domain experts and used consistently in the model.

In domain-driven design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a particular domain model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while outside that boundary the same words may have different meanings in other models.
DDD favors a rich domain model where behavior lives in the entities themselves; the anemic model is widely considered an anti-pattern.
In Domain-Driven Design, each bounded context owns an independent model, so identically named concepts in different contexts are distinct classes with their own meanings.
Symfony's Dependency Injection container instantiates services on first access (lazy) rather than all at once at boot, unless they are explicitly eager or a compiler pass forces instantiation.
The debug:router Symfony console command lists all registered routes of the application.

Autowiring automatically resolves constructor dependencies from type hints, and classes under src/ are auto-registered by default via resource-based service discovery, so you only need explicit configuration for exceptions and special cases.
Twig compiles templates into optimized PHP classes and caches them to avoid recompilation on subsequent requests.
In dev, ConfigCache::isFresh() only stats the resources (tracked files) dumped into the .meta file, so the container is rebuilt lazily only when one of them has a newer mtime, not on every request.
APP_ENV is the environment variable used to select the active Symfony environment (e.g. dev, prod).
Symfony's controller resolver verifies the action with is_callable(), which fails for private methods, so controller actions must be public.
Symfony registers both subscribers and listeners as tagged services, so their execution order depends on priority rather than on the interface itself.
Symfony 6.0 removed the legacy Guard authenticator system, leaving the new Authenticator-based system (Security's AuthenticatorInterface) as the standard.
The IsGranted attribute from the Security bundle denies access with a 403 when the current user lacks the given role or attribute.
Symfony's authorization system uses voter classes to decide whether a user is granted a specific attribute (like 'EDIT') on a given object such as $post.
Symfony 7 removed doctrine annotation support, so validation constraints are declared using native PHP attributes.
Symfony's Form component enables CSRF protection by default via the 'csrf_protection' option, validating the token on submission.
Symfony always runs its validator on the server during form handling, regardless of any client-side HTML5 constraint checks.
The Symfony MakerBundle command `make:form` interactively generates a FormType class.
Symfony stores only a serialized security token (containing user identifier/roles, not the plain-text password) in the session.
In modern Symfony applications, config/packages/ holds one configuration file per bundle or topic (e.g. framework.yaml, security.yaml).
It's a common convention to commit a .env with safe development defaults while keeping real secrets in a git-ignored .env.local file.
The debug:container command dumps all registered services and their aliases from the dependency injection container.

The compiled Container still inherits a public setParameter() that mutates the parameter bag, so later getParameter() calls return the new value — though services already instantiated keep the value they were injected with.
Since Symfony 4, services are private by default and must be explicitly marked public to be fetched directly from the container.
Most bundles provide default configuration and work fine without a config file; configuration is optional.
Symfony uses the %env(VAR)% placeholder syntax in configuration files like services.yaml to resolve environment variable values at runtime.
APP_DEBUG controls whether debug mode (profiler, verbose errors, Twig debug) is enabled.
Symfony Messenger allows multiple handlers to be registered for the same message, and all matching handlers are invoked.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process during send(), without dispatching it to a transport or waiting for a worker.
In Symfony the console command messenger:consume starts a worker that processes queued Messenger messages.
In Symfony Messenger, retry_strategy is set under each transport's options in config, so retry behavior is defined per transport.
By default Messenger uses PHP's native serialize()/unserialize() via the PhpSerializer; JSON encoding requires configuring the Serializer component.
Symfony Scheduler is built on top of Messenger and periodically produces messages into the bus according to configured cron-like schedules.
The doctrine transport persists and retrieves messages in database tables using the Doctrine ORM.
Symfony Messenger buses allow configuring custom middleware in the middleware stack before or after the built-in ones like SendMessageMiddleware or HandleMessageMiddleware.
Symfony follows this release policy with major versions every two years and minor versions each May and November.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.4 or higher as its minimum supported PHP version.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for Doctrine annotations, leaving PHP 8 attributes as the only option for validation and routing metadata.
AssetMapper maps assets without Node.js or build tools, using the importmap.php configuration file for JS/CSS dependencies.
Symfony 6.4 is a long-term support (LTS) release, providing extended bug and security fixes.
In Symfony, deprecations introduced in the previous major branch are removed when the next major release comes out.
Symfony includes UPGRADE guides (e.g., UPGRADE-5.0.md) documenting breaking changes for each major release.
The AssetMapper component compiles and serves assets and manages the importmap without requiring Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release in late November 2026 (8.1 came in May 2026), so it was not yet released on 2026-11-07.
Symfony releases minor versions every six months (8.0 in Nov 2025, 8.1 in May 2026), so 8.2 falls in November 2026.
Symfony follows a yearly release cycle in November, so 8.2 follows 8.1 as of November 2026.
Symfony 8.2 is a minor (backward-compatible) release; only major versions like 8.0 introduce breaking API changes.
A minor version bump (8.1 → 8.2) within the same major version follows semantic versioning, so backward compatibility is maintained and no code changes are required.
Symfony releases a new major alongside the previous branch's .4 LTS version, so 8.4 (November 2027) is the final minor of the 8.x line, shipped together with 9.0.
Symfony 8.x keeps its minimum at PHP 8.4 for the whole major; only the next major (Symfony 9) is expected to raise the requirement to PHP 8.5.
In the Symfony 8.x branch, deprecations for features scheduled for removal in 8.x will already be removed within that version, while only deprecations targeting 9.0 would persist until then.
Twig's {{ }} only evaluates Twig template expressions (variables, filters, functions), not arbitrary raw PHP code.
Twig enables auto-escaping by default using the HTML escaping strategy for templates ending in .html, .xml, and .svg.
The Twig |e filter escapes a string using the HTML escaping strategy by default, making it safe for output in an HTML context.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a given locale using intl.
The Twig |raw filter marks the value as safe HTML, so auto-escaping is not applied to it.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs the result of an expression, while {% %} is used for control structures like if, for, and set.
Twig supports the set tag ({% set var = value %}) to declare variables within a template, and loops, filters, and macros can also produce values.
The dump() Twig function outputs the debug structure of a variable such as an array or object.
Bootstrap is a front-end toolkit of prebuilt CSS and JavaScript components (modals, navbars, etc.) and does not provide SPA routing or state management.
The .container class in Bootstrap sets a responsive fixed max-width at each breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always 100% wide.
The Bootstrap grid splits a row into 12 columns (and modern versions use flexbox rather than floats).
Bootstrap has six grid breakpoints (xs, sm, md, lg, xl, xxl), but xs is the base with no infix, so only sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl appear as class-name infixes.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities multiply the $spacer variable (default 1rem) by the number, so .mt-3 equals 3 × $spacer.
In Bootstrap 5, data-bs-toggle activates interactive components like dropdowns, modals, and tabs.
Bootstrap 5 dropped its jQuery dependency and rewrites its components in vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM never generates tables automatically at runtime; you must explicitly run schema tools like doctrine:schema:create or migrations.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for insertion, and no SQL is executed until flush() is called.
The merge() method was removed in Doctrine ORM 3 (deprecated in 2.x), and even when it existed it returned a new managed copy rather than making the passed object itself managed.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) operates on entity classes and their fields rather than database tables and columns.
Repository find methods return null when no matching record is found.
Doctrine requires explicit calls to flush() to persist changes; no automatic flushing happens at request end.
In Doctrine ORM, a managed entity is already tracked by the Unit of Work, so flush() detects and commits property changes via change tracking without needing persist().
remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the actual DELETE query is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC allows readers and writers to proceed concurrently without blocking each other, though writers can still block each other.
The EXPLAIN command returns the query's execution plan without actually running the query.

SERIAL only creates a plain column with a default nextval() from a sequence, while GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY ties an internal sequence to the column with stricter rules (e.g., explicit inserts require OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, and the default cannot be altered), so they behave differently.
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct by default, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL in the column.
The string_agg(value, delimiter) PostgreSQL function concatenates strings using a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead-tuple space as reusable within the table; returning it to the OS requires VACUUM FULL (which rewrites the table).
The PARTITION BY clause in a window function divides the result set into groups (partitions) over which the window function is computed.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads, since previously read rows can be changed and committed by another transaction between reads.
In PostgreSQL, if no explicit transaction block is started, each statement is implicitly wrapped in its own transaction that is automatically committed or rolled back.
COMMIT ends the current transaction and permanently saves all changes made within it.

Indexes speed up locating rows for any query with a WHERE clause, so UPDATE and DELETE that filter on an indexed column find their target rows faster, even though maintaining the index itself adds some overhead.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, allowing partial rollback within a transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real execution times, whereas plain EXPLAIN only shows the plan without executing it.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector data type and indexing support for similarity search over embeddings.
A partial index includes only the rows that satisfy the WHERE clause, making it smaller and faster to maintain.

PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects read/write dependencies via predicates and uses an SIREAD lock concept rather than physically locking read rows.
HTTP status 201 (Created) indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in a new resource being created on the server.
204 No Content indicates the request succeeded and there is no body to return, commonly used for DELETE operations.
RFC 7231 defines DELETE as idempotent, since the effect of deleting a resource once is the same as deleting it any number of times (the resource is simply gone).
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server in its response, not by the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access the resource.
HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests) is the standard response indicating a client has exceeded the server's rate limit.
It's the opposite: 4xx status codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the body in a request or response.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas PUT requests must be idempotent.
Plain == can be vulnerable to timing attacks, so use hash_equals() for a constant-time comparison.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, tied to the user's session, and validated on the server for unsafe requests like POST.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header is used to enable and configure a site's CSP policy.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework — the access token grants access to resources, not identity; authentication is handled by something like OpenID Connect.
XSS must be prevented by context-aware output encoding/escaping when rendering data, not merely by validating input on the server before storing it.

In the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, the authorization server redirects to redirect_uri with a code parameter, which the client then exchanges (with client credentials) for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens without re-authenticating the user.
A salt is stored alongside the hash and only needs to be unique, not secret, since a stolen salt doesn't help reverse a secure hash.
PHPUnit only discovers and runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (or its subclasses).
setUp() runs before each test method, while setUpBeforeClass() runs once before all tests of the class.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, causing the test to run once for each data set.
The expectException() method tells PHPUnit to expect an exception of the given class to be thrown during the test.
It's the reverse: a mock sets expectations and verifies method calls, while a stub only provides canned return values.
PHPUnit 10 introduced the #[DataProvider] attribute and deprecated the @dataProvider annotation in favor of attributes.
PHPUnit tests should be independent so that one test's result does not affect another's.
The --order-by=random option (also accepting --order=random) makes PHPUnit run test cases in a random order.
